newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila's 'king of the road' threatened by wealth.
newsitem.headline: Manila's 'king of the road' threatened by wealth.

text.p: You can't miss them -- elongated, low-slung, chrome-plated vans, belching smoke and lurching from one lane to another as their passengers cringe and other drivers scramble out of the way.

Born from surplus U.S. equipment after World War Two, the jeepney has survived half a century in the toughest conditions. But the existence of this respected -- and reviled -- national symbol is now threatened by a formidable enemy: prosperity.
Wealthy Filipinos who usually brave Manila's traffic chaos without a qualm have been known to lapse into profanities at the sight of a jeepney ahead of their sleek imported cars.
But the irreverence of the rich towards this vehicle that is the backbone of the Philippines' public transport system, is more than offset by the services it provides to millions.
The differences over the jeepney symbolise the Philippines' dilemma as the country tries to pole-vault from the ranks of the poor to the ranks of East Asian tiger economies.

"I have recommended in 1994 that jeepneys should be phased out from Metro Manila. They carry much fewer people than a bus but take much road space and cause problems," said Manila's chief traffic controller, Romeo Maganto.
But officials have failed to tame the feisty drivers or their garish jeepneys, which have been tourist attractions.
"... they have very strong jeepney associations. They immediately go on the streets. They go on strike," Maganto said.
DRIVERS ALSO CARRY POLITICAL CLOUT
Manila's four jeepney associations, comprising owners as well as drivers, have about 270,000 members and are a formidable vote bank that no politician dare rile.
In fact, Philippine vice-president Joseph Estrada, popularly known as Erap, is campaigning for the 1998 presidential elections through a radio programme called Jeep ni Erap.
The jeepney was conceived by ingenious Filipinos in war-ravaged Manila after U.S.forces abandoned their jeeps.
Leonardo Sarao, now in his seventies, was one of those who gave up driving horse-drawn carriages after converting the military jeeps into utility vehicles.
"What he did was to cut the American jeep in the middle, extend the chassis and the roof so it could accommodate more people," said Sarao's son, Leonardo Sarao Jr.
Since it was cheap to make, cost little to run and was durable on the roughest of roads, the jeepney soon became the mainstay of Philippine transport.
The Saraos soon set up Sarao Motors Inc, where jeepneys still are manufactured completely indigenously.

Although there are no more surplus jeeps here, the vehicle's shape has become popular, keeping some 250 workers busy bashing sheets of metal into the same shape and fitting them with second-hand truck engines.

In the cities, jeepneys ferry thousands of office workers. In the countryside they swing down dusty roads with a dozen passengers and parcels crammed inside. Other passengers sit on the roof with baskets of produce, and more cling to the sides.
"In our heyday, we used to make nine jeepneys a day, but now there is a slump and we make about three," Sarao Jr said.
He blamed the slump on deregulation. "Now everyone comes here to invest and make cars. We now have 22 car manufacturers in the Philippines," he said.
NO MATCH FOR THE AUTO GIANTS
Sarao and other jeepney makers are no match for the Japanese and Korean automobile giants.
Their only advantage is price. Jeepneys are made with used truck engines fitted onto a simple chassis, and the body is hand-built from plain iron sheets.

Asked if the jeepney would survive, Sarao said: "If our country remains a poor country, the jeepney will stay. But if it will become a country which you might regard as a tiger economy, I think there will be bleak prospects for the jeepney."
The vast majority of Filipinos still use the jeepney. But with the country's increasing prosperity, many now prefer air-conditioned buses and taxis.
And another threat looms: government plans to build a light rail network will soon give Manila a mass transport system.
